title: IP Address Lookup: Where an Address Sits
description: Look up an IP address's approximate location, ISP and network with the IP Address Lookup — city-level, honestly scoped. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a lookup can usually name the country and often the city region an address routes through — but the street address it can never give you is the one thing it is most often asked for.
quick_answer: The IP Address Lookup reports what an IP address can honestly reveal: its approximate geographic area (country, usually region or city), the network or ISP it belongs to, and its technical registration details. Enter the address and read the record — network geography, not a person's location.
steps_intro: An IP address is a network fact. Read it as one:

body.t: Sign-ins and firewall hits from an unexpected country are the lookup's daily bread — context for a decision, not the decision itself (the
page shows the reader their own address for comparison).
An order whose IP geography contradicts its billing country earns a second look — one signal among several, weighted like one.
Traffic arriving from the wrong continent usually means a VPN, a proxy or a cloud region choice — the lookup names the exit, and the configuration explains it.
Yes, you can look up the address in that email header. What you learn is its network's geography — the sender's street remains, correctly, none of this tool's business.

IP geolocation databases map address blocks to the places ISPs route them from. A result naming a city means 'this block is administered/routed around there' — for many users that is their city; for mobile and satellite users it may be a hub hundreds of miles away.
Your office is in Ohio; the lookup says Amsterdam. That is not an error — it is the VPN exit doing exactly what it was bought to do, and the lookup reading the network honestly.

faq: Varies by network: fixed broadband in well-mapped countries is often right at city level; mobile carrier addresses resolve to gateway cities that can be far from the handset. Treat city results as the network's centre of gravity, not the device's position.
Both look up; IPv6 databases are younger and sometimes coarser geographically. The address family is reported with the result so the confidence reads correctly.
Can I locate an email sender this way?
You can locate the sending server's network from the header's originating address — usually their provider's infrastructure, which for webmail is a data centre, not a person.
Is looking up an IP legal?

Looking up publicly registered network information is a routine, lawful network operation (the same data WHOIS publishes). Using it to harass or stalk is neither this tool's purpose nor a capability its data actually grants.
Why does the same IP show two cities in two tools?
Different databases, different refresh dates, different ISP submissions. Disagreement between providers is the data's normal state; the country almost always agrees even when the city does not.
What is a private or reserved address?
Ranges like 192.168.x.x and 10.x.x.x exist only inside local networks — they have no public geography to look up, and the lookup says so instead of inventing one.
Does the tool store queried addresses?
Queries are processed to answer them. Prudent practice stands regardless: an IP you would not post publicly is one to query thoughtfully anywhere.
A Tor exit or open proxy resolves to the exit machine's network — the design working as intended. The lookup reports the exit's geography and flags the pattern where the data supports it.
